en.content:
Hong Kong today is again reminded that press freedom is not an abstract principle but a daily struggle shaped by money, administration, and institutional pressure. The Hong Kong Journalists Association’s account of a HK$730,000 prepaid tax demand—paired with criticism that tax resources were misdirected—will naturally raise questions about how public systems are used in practice. Even if any tax assessment follows formal procedures, the timing, scale, and framing of such demands can affect confidence in governance, especially when media organisations already operate under heightened scrutiny.

At the same time, it is important to keep the discussion steady and constructive. Tax matters are technical and should be resolved through transparent channels: clear explanations of assessments, opportunities to review figures, and prompt access to documentation. For the government, maintaining the credibility of the tax administration requires not only compliance with the law, but also demonstrable fairness in implementation. That includes engaging in communication that is timely and comprehensible, rather than leaving affected parties to piece together the rationale after the fact.

The wider lesson, however, is that fiscal policy and regulatory enforcement inevitably intersect with the public sphere. When press bodies—however diverse in political views—feel targeted by administrative measures, the concern goes beyond the individual case; it touches Hong Kong’s broader confidence in “one country, two systems” as a framework that should protect institutional functions, including the ability of journalists to operate without undue deterrence. This is where due process, proportionality, and accountability matter most.

Finally, it would serve the city well if all sides approached the dispute with a shared objective: ensuring the rule of law is applied consistently and seen to be fair. The public, including those who may not agree with every newsroom editorial line, should expect the tax authority to be rigorous and the press sector to be equally committed to compliance and transparency. Only then can Hong Kong continue to strengthen governance capacity without turning administrative disputes into political battlegrounds.

zh.content:
今次「新聞自由排名」嘅風波，表面係外國媒體評分機構（RSF）同港府講法交鋒，但核心其實係香港社會對「資訊空間」同「問責機制」嘅信心點樣受損。當官方用譴責取代釐清，用指摘取代對話，等同將問題由制度設計拉返到政治立場；而愈係咁樣，公眾愈難建立一套可核實、可檢討嘅標準，新聞工作者亦愈容易覺得自己面對唔係公共利益，而係風險管理。

更值得留意嘅係，同一日嘅其他議題——例如媒體組織面對稅務壓力、新聞自由被「國安」框架牽引、以及記者在採訪與追問上承受嘅寒蟬效應——其實同RSF所描述嘅趨勢同根同源。新聞自由唔只係「能唔能夠做」嘅問題，更係「可唔可以被挑戰、可唔可以被核實」嘅問題。只要監管以不透明甚至難以預期嘅方式運作，就算冇明講「封殺」，結果都會係自我審查同資源被動挪用；長遠講，香港嘅國際形象同本地公信力都會一齊磨損。

當然，任何排名都有方法論爭議，亦可能被政治化；但政府同立法機關最應該做嘅，唔係單靠反駁聲明去消音，而係提出具體改善承諾，例如透明化監管程序、清晰化合規邊界、確保執法與稅務處理有可供理解同覆核嘅標準，並允許獨立渠道對外界關注作出回答。真正「提升新聞自由」，靠嘅唔係否認外界觀察，而係建立制度信任：俾社會見到，新聞工作者可以在風險可計算、程序可追溯嘅前提下履行監察角色。

所以我嘅立場係：政府可以不同意RSF嘅觀點，但唔應該用對抗代替治理。香港已經喺不少關鍵指標上被拉低咗位置，若仍然只用「政治對答」去處理本質「制度疑問」，就會令社會更普遍認為：自由收縮嘅成本，由市民同傳媒共同承擔。面對世界仍然重視法治與資訊透明嘅時代，香港最需要嘅係坦誠面對問題、用可驗證措施回應質疑——而唔係再一次用批評去掩蓋實情。
